slides.title: Some things stay private
slides.text: Your full name, home address, phone number, school, and birthday are personal information. If a game asks for them, stop and check with a grown-up before typing anything.

widgetConfig.scenario: A new app asks for your full name, home address, and phone number. Should you share these?

options.label: No — these are personal details that should stay private
options.outcome: Exactly right! Your full name, home address, phone number, school, and birthday are personal information that should stay private.

options.label: Yes, sharing all your details is fine for any app
options.outcome: Sharing personal details with any app isn't safe — this information should stay private.

options.label: Only your address matters, the rest is fine to share
options.outcome: All of these details — name, address, phone, school, birthday — are personal and should stay private, not just your address.

slides.title: Keep your password secret
slides.text: A password is like a key that opens your account. Keep it between you and the grown-up who helps manage your account—not friends or people you meet in games.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend at school asks for your tablet password so they can play a game. What should you do?

options.label: Keep it private, even from friends
options.outcome: Right! Passwords should stay secret, even from friends — that keeps your things safe.

options.label: Tell them since they're a friend
options.outcome: Even friends shouldn't know your password — it's safest to keep it private.

options.label: Write it down and give it to them
options.outcome: Passwords are meant to stay secret, even from friends, to keep your account safe.

slides.title: Keep where you are private
slides.text: People online do not need to know where you live, go to school, or play. For example, do not tell a game-chat stranger the name of your school or park.

widgetConfig.scenario: A stranger in a game chat asks what school you go to. What should you do?

options.label: Don't tell them — keep that private
options.outcome: Exactly right! People online do not need to know where you live, go to school, or play.

options.label: Tell them right away
options.outcome: Telling a stranger online where you go to school isn't safe — that kind of information should stay private.

options.label: Where you live or go to school never needs to stay private
options.outcome: That information actually does need to stay private, especially from people you only know online.

slides.title: Have a grown-up nearby
slides.text: When you are still learning to use apps and games, a grown-up can help if something confusing pops up. If a message makes you worried, show it to them instead of handling it alone.

widgetConfig.scenario: A confusing message pops up while you're using an app. What should you do?

options.label: Show it to a grown-up instead of handling it alone
options.outcome: Exactly right! A grown-up can help if something confusing pops up — show it to them instead of handling it alone.

options.label: Figure it out completely by yourself
options.outcome: You don't have to figure it out alone — a grown-up can help with something confusing or worrying.

options.label: Grown-ups never need to know about confusing messages
options.outcome: Grown-ups actually should know about confusing or worrying messages — they can help.

slides.title: Ask before you post
slides.text: Before you share a photo, video, or comment, ask a grown-up. They can help notice private details in the background, such as your school name or house number.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to post a cute picture of you and your friend online. What should you do first?

options.label: Ask a grown-up and your friend if it's okay
options.outcome: Yes! Checking first keeps everyone comfortable and safe.

options.label: Post it right away since it's cute
options.outcome: Even cute pictures should get an okay first — not everyone wants their picture posted.

options.label: Post it but don't tell anyone
options.outcome: Asking first, not after, is what keeps it safe and respectful.

slides.title: Pictures can travel
slides.text: A photo can be copied, saved, or sent to other people after you share it. That is why it is smart to ask before posting—even if you only meant one friend to see it.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to post a photo meaning only one friend to see it. Could it still travel further?

options.label: Yes — it can be copied, saved, or sent to others
options.outcome: Exactly right! A photo can be copied, saved, or sent to other people after you share it, even if you only meant one friend to see it.

options.label: No, a photo always stays only with the one person you send it to
options.outcome: A photo doesn't always stay with just one person — it can be copied or sent further than you meant.

options.label: Photos can never be copied or shared further
options.outcome: Photos actually can be copied and shared further — that's exactly why it's smart to ask before posting.

slides.title: Your birthday and school are private too
slides.text: A birthday or school name can tell strangers more about you than you think. Share those details only with people your family trusts.

widgetConfig.scenario: An app you don't know asks for your birthday and the name of your school. What should you do?

options.label: Don't share it, and check with a grown-up first
options.outcome: Exactly right! Your birthday and school name can tell strangers more than you'd think — always check with a grown-up before sharing.

options.label: Share it since it's not your full address
options.outcome: Even without your address, details like your birthday and school can reveal more than you'd think — check with a grown-up first.

options.label: Share it if the app looks fun and colorful
options.outcome: A fun-looking app doesn't mean it's safe to share details with — always check with a grown-up first.

slides.title: Video calls need a check first
slides.text: Before starting a video call, make sure a grown-up knows who you are talking to. A camera can show your face, your room, and things around your home.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to start a video call. What should happen first?

options.label: A grown-up should know who you are talking to
options.outcome: Exactly right! Before starting a video call, make sure a grown-up knows who you are talking to.

options.label: Just start the call with no one knowing
options.outcome: Starting a video call with no one knowing isn't safe — a grown-up should know who you're talking to first.

options.label: Video calls never need any check beforehand
options.outcome: Video calls actually do need a check first, since a camera can show your face, room, and things around your home.

slides.title: Passwords protect your things
slides.text: Think of your password as the lock on a treasure box. A strong secret password helps keep your games, pictures, and messages safe.

widgetConfig.scenario: What does a strong password do for your games, pictures, and messages?

options.label: Keeps them safe, like a lock on a treasure box
options.outcome: Exactly right! Think of your password as the lock on a treasure box — a strong secret password helps keep your things safe.

options.label: Nothing — passwords do not actually protect anything
options.outcome: Passwords actually do protect your things — they're like the lock on a treasure box.

options.label: Passwords only matter for grown-ups, not kids
options.outcome: Passwords matter for kids too — they help keep games, pictures, and messages safe for everyone.

quiz.question: Should you share your full name and address on a screen?
choices: No, that stays private
Yes, anytime someone asks
quiz.explanation: Your name and address help people find you in real life. Like giving a stranger directions to your house.

quiz.question: Who should be nearby when you use a tablet or computer?
choices: A grown-up
Nobody — it's fine to be totally alone
quiz.explanation: A grown-up nearby can help if something goes wrong. Like a scary pop-up or message.

quiz.question: Once you post a picture online, can it be shared by others too?
choices: Yes, it can be saved or shared even more than you expect
No, only you can ever see it
quiz.explanation: A picture you post can be saved and passed along by others. Like a note passed around a classroom.

quiz.question: Should you share your password with someone you don't know?
choices: No, keep it secret
Yes, if they ask nicely
quiz.explanation: A password is a secret key to your stuff. Only your grown-up should ever have a copy.

quiz.question: Is it okay to tell people online exactly where you live?
choices: No, that stays with your family
Yes, that's fine to share
quiz.explanation: Where you live is a family secret. Strangers do not need to know it.

quiz.question: Should you ask a grown-up before posting a photo or video?
choices: Yes, always ask first
No, just post anything
quiz.explanation: A grown-up can spot things you might miss, like a photo showing your school.

quiz.question: Is your birthday okay to tell everyone online?
choices: Yes, tell everyone
No, that's private too
quiz.explanation: Your birthday is private too, just like your address. Save it for family and friends.

quiz.question: You want to video chat with someone. What should you do?
choices: Make sure a grown-up knows first
Just start chatting alone
quiz.explanation: A grown-up should always know who is on the screen. Like knowing who is at the door.

quiz.question: What is a password like?
choices: A secret code just for you and your family
Something to tell all your friends
quiz.explanation: A password is like a secret code just for you. It keeps your things locked and safe.

quiz.question: You take a photo of your friend. Before sharing it, what should you do?
choices: Ask a grown-up and your friend first
Share it right away with everyone
quiz.explanation: Ask your friend and a grown-up first. Like asking before you borrow a toy.

slides.title: If something feels weird
slides.text: If a video, message, picture, or person online makes you feel scared, confused, or uncomfortable, stop and tell a grown-up. You will not be in trouble for asking for help.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're using an app and someone online asks you a question that makes you feel a little weird or uncomfortable. What should you do?

options.label: Tell a grown-up you trust right away
options.outcome: Yes! That weird feeling is important — telling a trusted grown-up is always the right move.

options.label: Keep it a secret and just ignore it
options.outcome: Keeping weird feelings secret can let problems continue. Telling a trusted grown-up helps keep you safe.

options.label: Answer the question so they stop asking
options.outcome: You never have to answer a question that makes you uncomfortable — tell a grown-up instead.

slides.title: People online can pretend
slides.text: A person online may use a different name or picture, so you cannot always know who they really are. Treat new online people like strangers until a grown-up helps you check.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone online says they're a kid your age, but something about how they talk seems off. What should you remember?

options.label: People online aren't always who they say they are
options.outcome: Exactly right — it's important to remember that people online can pretend to be someone they're not, so trusting a grown-up with concerns is always smart.

options.label: Everyone online is always honest about who they are
options.outcome: Not everyone online is honest about who they are — that's exactly why staying cautious and telling a grown-up matters.

options.label: It doesn't matter who they really are
options.outcome: It matters a lot — knowing people online can pretend helps you stay safe and know when to tell a trusted grown-up.

slides.title: Pause before you click
slides.text: Pop-ups and giant buttons are designed to make you click quickly. If you do not know what a button does, pause and ask before tapping it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A giant flashing button pops up saying 'Click here to win a prize!' What should you do?

options.label: Pause and ask a grown-up before clicking
options.outcome: Exactly right! Pop-ups and giant buttons are designed to make you click quickly — pausing to ask a grown-up is the safe move.

options.label: Click it immediately since it looks exciting
options.outcome: Clicking right away is exactly what flashy pop-ups are designed to get you to do — pausing first is safer.

options.label: Flashy pop-ups are always safe to click
options.outcome: Flashy pop-ups aren't always safe — pausing and checking with a grown-up first protects you.

slides.title: Use apps your family has checked
slides.text: Not every app, video, or game is made for kids. Use ones your family has approved, and ask before installing something new.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to try a new app. What should you do first?

options.label: Ask before installing something new
options.outcome: Exactly right! Not every app is made for kids — use ones your family has approved, and ask before installing something new.

options.label: Install anything without asking
options.outcome: Installing anything without asking skips an important safety step — asking first helps make sure it's okay.

options.label: Every app is automatically made for kids
options.outcome: Not every app is made for kids — that's exactly why asking and checking first matters.

slides.title: Game coins can cost real money
slides.text: Coins, skins, pets, and extra levels in a game can use real money. Even if it only takes one tap, ask before buying anything.

widgetConfig.scenario: A game offers coins or skins with one tap. Is this always free?

options.label: No — it can use real money, even with just one tap
options.outcome: Exactly right! Coins, skins, and extra levels in a game can use real money — even one tap, so ask before buying anything.

options.label: Yes, in-game purchases are always free
options.outcome: In-game purchases aren't always free — even a single tap can use real money.

options.label: Only buying things outside of games ever costs real money
options.outcome: In-game purchases can cost real money too, not just purchases outside of games.

slides.title: Screens need breaks too
slides.text: Your eyes, body, and brain need time away from screens. After playing for a while, stretch, look far away, get some water, or play offline.

widgetConfig.scenario: You've been playing on a screen for a while. What should you do?

options.label: Stretch, look far away, or play offline for a bit
options.outcome: Exactly right! Your eyes, body, and brain need time away from screens — stretching or playing offline helps.

options.label: Keep staring at the screen with no break
options.outcome: Staying on the screen with no break doesn't give your eyes and body the rest they need.

options.label: Breaks from screens are never necessary
options.outcome: Breaks from screens actually are necessary — your eyes, body, and brain need time away.

slides.title: You can always say no
slides.text: If someone in a game asks for a secret, a photo, personal information, or something that feels wrong, you can say no, leave, and tell a grown-up.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone in a game asks for a secret or personal information. What can you do?

options.label: Say no, leave, and tell a grown-up
options.outcome: Exactly right! If something feels wrong, you can say no, leave, and tell a grown-up.

options.label: Share it since they asked nicely
options.outcome: Being asked nicely doesn't mean you have to share — you can always say no if it feels wrong.

options.label: You must always answer whatever someone asks in a game
options.outcome: You never have to answer something that feels wrong — saying no and telling a grown-up is always okay.

slides.title: Flashy ads want your attention
slides.text: Some ads blink, move, or make loud sounds so you notice them. You do not have to click—close them or ask for help if you are unsure.

widgetConfig.scenario: An ad blinks and makes loud sounds to get your attention. Do you have to click it?

options.label: No — you can close it or ask for help
options.outcome: Exactly right! Some ads blink or make sounds on purpose, but you do not have to click — you can close them or ask for help.

options.label: Yes, you must always click flashy ads
options.outcome: You never have to click a flashy ad — you can close it or ask a grown-up for help.

options.label: Ads never try to grab your attention on purpose
options.outcome: Ads actually are designed on purpose to grab your attention, which is why it's okay to just close them.

slides.title: Choose shows that fit you
slides.text: Videos can appear automatically, and the next one may not be meant for kids. Use shows and channels your family has checked, and tell a grown-up if something upsetting appears.

widgetConfig.scenario: A video that's not meant for kids starts playing automatically. What should you do?

options.label: Tell a grown-up if something upsetting appears
options.outcome: Exactly right! Videos can play automatically and the next one may not be meant for kids — tell a grown-up if something upsetting appears.

options.label: Keep watching no matter what appears
options.outcome: Continuing to watch something upsetting isn't the right move — telling a grown-up helps.

options.label: Videos that play automatically are always fine for kids
options.outcome: Videos that autoplay aren't always meant for kids — telling a grown-up about anything upsetting matters.

quiz.question: A video suddenly shows something scary. What should you do?
choices: Tell a grown-up right away
Keep it a secret
quiz.explanation: Telling a grown-up helps fix the scary thing fast. Like calling for help when you are hurt.

quiz.question: Is everyone online always exactly who their picture says they are?
choices: No, that's not always true
Yes, always
quiz.explanation: A picture can belong to anyone, even a grown-up pretending to be a kid. That is why we stay careful.

quiz.question: A big flashing button suddenly says "click here now!" What should you do?
choices: Ask a grown-up first
Just click it right away
quiz.explanation: Flashy buttons try to trick you into clicking fast. Asking a grown-up first is always safer.

quiz.question: A friend tells you about a new game. What should you do before downloading it?
choices: Check with a grown-up first
Download any app at all, without asking
quiz.explanation: A grown-up checks that a game is safe first. Like checking a toy for sharp edges.

quiz.question: A game asks you to buy coins with money. What should you do?
choices: Ask a grown-up first
Buy it right away
quiz.explanation: Buying coins uses real money from your family. A grown-up should always say yes first.

quiz.question: You've been on a screen a long time and your eyes feel tired. What should you do?
choices: Keep playing without stopping
Take a break
quiz.explanation: Breaks let your eyes and body rest. Like resting after running around outside.

quiz.question: A game asks you to do something that feels wrong. What should you do?
choices: Say no and tell a grown-up
Do it anyway to keep playing
quiz.explanation: Saying no and telling a grown-up keeps you safe. Even if the game says otherwise.

quiz.question: An ad flashes big and loud saying "click now!" What should you do?
choices: You never have to click it
You must click it right away
quiz.explanation: Loud, flashy ads want your click. You never have to give it, like ignoring a shouting stranger.

quiz.question: Who helps pick safe shows and videos for you to watch?
choices: A grown-up
Nobody, you pick anything
quiz.explanation: Grown-ups check shows the same way they check games. They make sure it is okay for you.

quiz.question: You click a pop-up by accident. What should you do next?
choices: Tell a grown-up what happened
Keep clicking around to see what happens
quiz.explanation: Telling a grown-up right away helps fix mistakes fast. Even little ones, like an accidental click.

slides.title: What makes a password strong?
slides.text: A strong password is long and hard for someone else to guess. A made-up passphrase such as “PurpleRocket!River7” is safer than your name, birthday, pet name, or “123456.”

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap a button for each one

items.label: A random mix of words, numbers & symbols
A long made-up phrase only you know

slides.title: Privacy settings
slides.text: Privacy settings help control who can see your posts, photos, profile, or location. With a grown-up, set accounts so only people you actually know can see personal things.

widgetConfig.scenario: An app lets you control who can see your posts and photos. What are these controls called?

options.label: Privacy settings
options.outcome: Exactly right! Privacy settings help control who can see your posts, photos, and profile.

options.label: Game settings
options.outcome: Game settings control gameplay options — the controls over who sees your posts are called privacy settings.

options.label: There is no way to control who sees your posts
options.outcome: There actually is a way — privacy settings let you control exactly that.

slides.title: Keep your location private
slides.text: Your school, home, sports field, and live location can show strangers where to find you. Keep location sharing off unless you and a trusted grown-up intentionally need it.

widgetConfig.scenario: An app wants to share your live location. Should you turn this on by default?

options.label: No — keep location sharing off unless truly needed
options.outcome: Exactly right! Keep location sharing off unless you and a trusted grown-up intentionally need it.

options.label: Yes, always share your exact location
options.outcome: Sharing your live location by default isn't safe — your school, home, or field location can show strangers where to find you.

options.label: Location sharing never reveals anything important
options.outcome: Location sharing actually can reveal a lot, like where you live or play — it's worth keeping off by default.

slides.title: Think before you post
slides.text: Before posting, ask: “Would I be okay if a teacher, parent, or classmate saw this later?” If the answer is no or you are unsure, do not post it yet.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to post a photo showing your house number and street sign in the background. What should you do?

options.label: Crop or avoid posting photos that reveal your address
options.outcome: Smart thinking! Avoiding details like your address in photos helps protect your privacy.

options.label: Post it anyway since it's just a photo
options.outcome: Photos can accidentally reveal your address — it's safer to crop or avoid showing those details.

options.label: Add your exact address in the caption too
options.outcome: Sharing your exact address publicly is risky — it's safer to keep that information private.

slides.title: Log out on shared devices
slides.text: If other people use the same computer or tablet, log out when you are finished. Otherwise the next person could open your account, read messages, or change settings.

widgetConfig.scenario: You finish using a shared computer. What should you do?

options.label: Log out of your account
options.outcome: Exactly right! If other people use the same computer or tablet, log out when you are finished.

options.label: Leave it logged in for the next person
options.outcome: Leaving it logged in means the next person could open your account or change settings — logging out protects you.

options.label: Logging out on shared devices never matters
options.outcome: Logging out actually matters a lot on shared devices — it prevents the next person from accessing your account.

slides.title: Change a password if something feels wrong
slides.text: If someone may know your password, or your account acts strangely, tell a grown-up and change the password. It is like changing a lock when you think someone copied the key.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your account starts acting strangely. What should you do?

options.label: Tell a grown-up and change your password
options.outcome: Exactly right! If your account acts strangely, tell a grown-up and change the password — like changing a lock when you think someone copied the key.

options.label: Ignore it and hope it goes away
options.outcome: Ignoring strange account activity doesn't fix it — telling a grown-up and changing your password helps.

options.label: Strange account activity never means anything
options.outcome: Strange account activity can actually mean something real — it's worth telling a grown-up and changing your password.

slides.title: What “private account” really means
slides.text: A private account limits your posts to approved followers, but it cannot stop someone from taking a screenshot or sharing what they saw. Private is safer—not invisible.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your account is private, limited to approved followers. Does this mean nothing can ever be shared further?

options.label: No — someone could still screenshot and share it
options.outcome: Exactly right! A private account limits your posts to approved followers, but it cannot stop someone from taking a screenshot — private is safer, not invisible.

options.label: Yes, private means completely invisible to everyone
options.outcome: Private doesn't mean completely invisible — an approved follower could still screenshot and share what they saw.

options.label: Private accounts can never be screenshotted
options.outcome: Private accounts actually can still be screenshotted by someone who's approved to follow you.

slides.title: Pick usernames that reveal less
slides.text: A username does not need your real name, age, school, or birth year. “BlueFalcon27” gives away less than “EmmaMarlboro2017.”

widgetConfig.scenario: Which username gives away less personal information?

options.label: "BlueFalcon27"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A username does not need your real name, age, school, or birth year — 'BlueFalcon27' gives away much less than a name-based one.

options.label: "EmmaMarlboro2017"
options.outcome: This username gives away a real name and possibly a birth year — 'BlueFalcon27' reveals much less personal information.

options.label: Usernames never reveal anything personal
options.outcome: Usernames actually can reveal personal information, like a real name or birth year, depending on how they're chosen.

slides.title: If your account may be hacked
slides.text: Signs can include strange messages, password-change emails you did not request, or suddenly being locked out. Tell a grown-up, change your password, and use the app’s account-recovery tools.

widgetConfig.scenario: You get password-change emails you never requested. What should you do?

options.label: Tell a grown-up, change your password, use account-recovery tools
options.outcome: Exactly right! Signs like unrequested password-change emails mean you should tell a grown-up, change your password, and use account-recovery tools.

options.label: Ignore the emails completely
options.outcome: Ignoring these emails could let a real problem go unaddressed — telling a grown-up and changing your password is safer.

options.label: Unexpected password-change emails never mean anything
options.outcome: Unexpected password-change emails can actually be a real warning sign worth acting on.

quiz.question: Which is a stronger password: "password123" or "BlueTiger$7Jump"?
choices: "BlueTiger$7Jump," since it's harder to guess
"password123," since it's easier to remember
quiz.explanation: Simple passwords like 'password123' are easy for a computer program to guess in seconds. Mixing letters, numbers, and symbols, like 'BlueTiger$7Jump,' makes a password much harder to crack.

quiz.question: What do privacy settings let you control?
choices: Who can see what you post
How fast your device charges
quiz.explanation: Privacy settings decide who can see your posts and photos, similar to choosing who's invited to a party. Setting yours to 'friends only' keeps strangers out.

quiz.question: Should you share your exact location with people you don't know well?
choices: No, keep that private
Yes, it's fine to share with anyone
quiz.explanation: Your exact location tells someone exactly where to find you, even someone you've never met. Keeping it private, like your school or the park you play at, keeps you safer.

quiz.question: You use a shared computer at school. What should you do when you're done?
choices: Log out of your account
Leave it logged in for the next person
quiz.explanation: Staying logged in lets the next person open your messages or even change your password. Logging out, like locking a door when you leave, keeps your account just yours.

quiz.question: Before posting a photo or comment, what's a smart first step?
choices: Think about who might see it, or ask a grown-up
Post it immediately without thinking
quiz.explanation: Once something is posted, people you never expected might see it, like a teacher or a stranger. Thinking ahead, or asking a grown-up, helps you decide if it's really okay to share.

quiz.question: You think someone else might know your password. What should you do?
choices: Tell a grown-up so you can change it
Do nothing and hope it's fine
quiz.explanation: If someone else knows your password, they could log in and pretend to be you. Changing it with a grown-up, like changing a lock after losing a key, fixes that.

quiz.question: What does a private account setting do?
choices: It lets anyone in the world see your posts
Only approved followers can see your posts
quiz.explanation: A private account only shows your posts to people you've approved, unlike a public one anyone can find. It's like a photo album only your friends are allowed to open.

quiz.question: Which username reveals less personal information: "SoccerStar2013" or "BlueFalcon99"?
choices: "BlueFalcon99"
"SoccerStar2013", since it mentions a sport
quiz.explanation: Usernames like 'SoccerStar2013' can hint at your birth year, giving strangers an extra clue about your age. A name like 'BlueFalcon99' keeps that kind of detail hidden.

quiz.question: Friends say you're posting strange messages you didn't write. What might this mean?
choices: Your account might be hacked
Nothing, that's completely normal
quiz.explanation: Strange messages you didn't write, like weird links sent from your account, are a sign someone else got in. Telling a grown-up quickly helps get your account back safely.

quiz.question: A friend asks for your game account password so they can log in for you. What should you do?
choices: Say no, passwords stay private
Share it since they're your friend
quiz.explanation: Passwords are meant to stay secret, even from close friends, since you can't control what they do once they have it. Saying no protects your account either way.

slides.title: Online strangers are still strangers
slides.text: Someone you meet in a game may seem friendly, but you still do not know who is behind the screen. Do not share your school, address, phone number, passwords, or private photos.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone you've never met messages you in a game and asks to be "best online friends" right away. What should you do?

options.label: Stay cautious — they're still a stranger, even online
options.outcome: Exactly right. Someone being friendly online doesn't change the fact that you don't actually know them.

options.label: Treat them like a close friend immediately
options.outcome: Online strangers are still strangers, even if they seem nice — it takes time (and a grown-up's input) to know if someone is safe.

options.label: Share personal details so they trust you back
options.outcome: Sharing personal info with someone you just met online isn't safe, no matter how friendly they seem.

slides.title: Kindness counts online
slides.text: A real person reads the words you type. Before sending a comment, imagine saying it face-to-face—if it would be cruel in person, it is cruel online too.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to type a harsh comment. What's a good test before sending it?

options.label: Imagine saying it to the person's face
options.outcome: Exactly right! A real person reads what you type — if it would be cruel in person, it is cruel online too.

options.label: Send it since it is just online, not in person
options.outcome: Something cruel online is still cruel, even if it's not said face-to-face — imagining saying it in person is a good test.

options.label: Kindness never matters in online comments
options.outcome: Kindness actually matters just as much online as in person, since a real person reads what you type.

slides.title: Block, save, and tell
slides.text: If someone is mean or keeps bothering you, do not start a fight back. Save evidence if needed, block or report the account, and tell a trusted grown-up.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone online keeps being mean to you. What should you do?

options.label: Save evidence, block or report, and tell a trusted grown-up
options.outcome: Exactly right! If someone is mean or keeps bothering you, save evidence if needed, block or report the account, and tell a trusted grown-up.

options.label: Start a fight back
options.outcome: Fighting back can make things worse — blocking, saving evidence, and telling a grown-up is a safer response.

options.label: Handle it completely alone with no one else involved
options.outcome: You don't have to handle it alone — telling a trusted grown-up is an important part of responding well.

slides.title: Be careful with downloads
slides.text: A “free” game, mod, or file from an unfamiliar site can contain unwanted software or scams. Ask before installing, and use trusted app stores or official sites.

widgetConfig.scenario: A website offers a free download of a popular game that normally costs money. What should you do?

options.label: Be suspicious — ask a grown-up before downloading anything like that
options.outcome: Smart thinking — free downloads of normally-paid things are a common way harmful software gets onto devices. Checking with a grown-up first is the safe move.

options.label: Download it right away since it's free
options.outcome: Unexpected free downloads of paid things are a common trick — checking with a grown-up first helps keep your device safe.

options.label: Download it and share the link with friends
options.outcome: Sharing a risky download spreads the risk to friends too — it's safer to check with a grown-up first.

slides.title: Links can pretend to be prizes
slides.text: Messages such as “You won—click now!” may be trying to steal information or install something unsafe. Do not click surprise links; check with a grown-up first.

widgetConfig.scenario: A message says "You won — click now!" Should you click it right away?

options.label: No — check with a grown-up first
options.outcome: Exactly right! Messages like this may be trying to steal information — do not click surprise links, check with a grown-up first.

options.label: Yes, always click surprise prize links immediately
options.outcome: Clicking surprise prize links right away can be risky — checking with a grown-up first is much safer.

options.label: Surprise prize links are always completely safe
options.outcome: Surprise prize links are often not safe — they can be trying to steal information or install something unsafe.

slides.title: Keep game chat about the game
slides.text: You can talk strategy without sharing personal details. A player does not need your real name, school, city, phone number, or where you are right now.

widgetConfig.scenario: A player in your game asks for your real name and city. Do they need this to play?

options.label: No — you can talk strategy without personal details
options.outcome: Exactly right! You can talk strategy without sharing personal details — a player doesn't need your real name, city, or phone number.

options.label: Yes, you must share personal details to play
options.outcome: You don't need to share personal details to play a game — strategy talk doesn't require your real name or city.

options.label: Personal details never matter in game chat
options.outcome: Personal details actually matter a lot in game chat — they're not needed to play and are safer kept private.

slides.title: In-app purchases use real money
slides.text: Game coins, skins, and upgrades may look imaginary, but the money charged is real. Ask before buying anything or starting a subscription.

widgetConfig.scenario: A game offers you special coins and skins to buy with one tap. Is this free?

options.label: No — those purchases use real money
options.outcome: Exactly right! Game coins and skins may look imaginary, but the money charged for them is real — always ask a grown-up first.

options.label: Yes, since it's all inside a game
options.outcome: Being inside a game doesn't make it free — those purchases charge real money.

options.label: It's only real money if it costs more than $10
options.outcome: Any amount charged for in-app purchases is real money, no matter how small it looks.

slides.title: Make room for offline life too
slides.text: Screens are fun, but they should not regularly push out sleep, homework, movement, family time, or activities you enjoy. If they do, it is time to rebalance.

widgetConfig.scenario: Screens are regularly pushing out sleep and family time. What should you do?

options.label: Rebalance so offline life gets room too
options.outcome: Exactly right! Screens should not regularly push out sleep, homework, movement, or family time — if they do, it's time to rebalance.

options.label: Keep screens as the only priority
options.outcome: Keeping screens as the only priority can crowd out sleep and family time — rebalancing helps make room for both.

options.label: Screens never affect sleep or other parts of life
options.outcome: Screens actually can affect sleep and other parts of life quite a bit, which is why rebalancing matters.

slides.title: Be extra careful with cameras
slides.text: Livestreams and video chats reveal more than text: your face, voice, room, and surroundings. Use them only with people you really know and with a trusted grown-up aware.

widgetConfig.scenario: A livestream or video chat shows your face, voice, and room. Who should you use this with?

options.label: Only people you really know, with a grown-up aware
options.outcome: Exactly right! Livestreams and video chats reveal more than text — use them only with people you really know and with a trusted grown-up aware.

options.label: Anyone at all, with no one else knowing
options.outcome: Using cameras with anyone at all, with no grown-up aware, isn't safe — reserve them for people you really know.

options.label: Cameras never reveal more than text messages do
options.outcome: Cameras actually reveal a lot more than text — your face, voice, room, and surroundings.

quiz.question: A stranger in a game chat asks what school you go to. Should you answer?
choices: No, just like in real life
Yes, it's completely different online
quiz.explanation: You wouldn't tell a stranger on the street your school name, so the same rule applies online. Staying quiet keeps that information safe.

quiz.question: Typing something mean online but not saying it in person — does it still hurt?
choices: No, it doesn't count if it's online
Yes, mean words hurt the same online
quiz.explanation: Words typed on a screen still reach a real person reading them, even if you can't see their face. That's why mean comments hurt just as much online.

quiz.question: Someone leaves a rude comment on your post. What's the safest response?
choices: Tell a grown-up and don't respond with meanness
Say something even meaner back
quiz.explanation: Telling a grown-up gets you real help, while typing something meaner back usually makes things worse for everyone. Staying calm and reporting it is the safer choice.

quiz.question: A message offers a "free game mod" from an unfamiliar website. What should you do?
choices: Check with a grown-up first
Download anything that looks fun immediately
quiz.explanation: Not every download is what it claims to be, since some hide viruses or scams inside. Checking with a grown-up before installing anything new keeps your device safe.

quiz.question: A pop-up says "you've won a free gaming console, click here!" What is it probably?
choices: A trick, not a real prize
Definitely a real, safe prize
quiz.explanation: Real prizes almost never arrive through a random pop-up from a stranger. A message like this is usually a trick to get you to click something unsafe.

quiz.question: A player in your online game asks what city you live in. What should you avoid sharing?
choices: Personal details
Your favorite game strategy
quiz.explanation: Even a friendly player in a game is still someone you've never actually met in person. Keeping details like your city private protects you, just like it would with any stranger.

quiz.question: A game button says "buy 500 coins for $4.99." What should you do first?
choices: Check with a grown-up first
Buy it right away without asking
quiz.explanation: Tapping 'buy' inside a game usually charges a real card linked to your family's account. Checking with a grown-up first makes sure that spending is okay.

quiz.question: You've been playing a game for hours and feel too tired for soccer practice. What might that mean?
choices: Your screen time might need balancing
Nothing, screens never affect how you feel
quiz.explanation: Feeling too tired for something you love, like soccer practice, can be a sign screen time crept up too high. Noticing that and cutting back helps you enjoy both.

quiz.question: An app lets you video chat with people you've never met. What should you do?
choices: Keep it to people you know and involve a grown-up for anything new
Video chat with anyone who asks
quiz.explanation: Cameras let strangers see your face and room in real time, which is more than a text message ever shows. Keeping video chats to people you actually know, with a grown-up aware, is safest.

quiz.question: A text message from an unknown number says "You won! Click this link fast!" What's the safest move?
choices: Don't click it — treat it as a trick
Click it quickly before the offer ends
quiz.explanation: Scammers create urgency, like a countdown or 'click fast,' to stop you from thinking it through. A surprise prize message from an unknown number is very likely a scam.

slides.title: What is phishing?
slides.text: Phishing is a fake message designed to make you reveal a password, code, or personal information. Example: “Your game account will be deleted—log in here now!” may lead to a copycat login page.

widgetConfig.scenario: You get an email saying you won a free gift card — just click the link and enter your info to claim it. What should you do?

options.label: Be suspicious and avoid clicking the link
options.outcome: Smart — surprise "you won!" messages asking you to click and enter info are a classic phishing trick.

options.label: Click the link right away to claim the prize
options.outcome: Clicking links in unexpected "you won" emails is exactly how phishing scams steal information — best to avoid them.

options.label: Forward it to friends so they can claim prizes too
options.outcome: Forwarding a phishing email spreads the scam to others — it's better to just delete or report it.

slides.title: Use two-step verification
slides.text: Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds another check after your password, such as an app code or device prompt. If someone steals your password, that second step can still block them.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your account offers an optional extra security step (like a code texted to your phone) when logging in. Should you turn it on?

options.label: Yes — it adds a strong extra layer of protection
options.outcome: Exactly! Two-step verification makes it much harder for someone else to get into your account, even if they somehow get your password.

options.label: No, one password is always enough
options.outcome: Passwords alone can be guessed or stolen — two-step verification adds real extra protection.

options.label: It's only for businesses, not personal accounts
options.outcome: Two-step verification is valuable for personal accounts too — it protects anyone's account from unauthorized access.

slides.title: Use strong, unique passwords
slides.text: Use a different strong password for important accounts. If one site is breached, reusing the same password can let attackers try it on your email, games, and social accounts too.

widgetConfig.scenario: You use the exact same password for every single account. If one site gets hacked, what happens?

options.label: All your other accounts using that password become at risk too
options.outcome: Exactly right! Reusing one password everywhere means a hack on one site can put all your other accounts at risk too.

options.label: Nothing — hacks never affect your other accounts
options.outcome: A hack can absolutely affect your other accounts if you reuse the same password — using unique passwords protects you.

options.label: Only that one site is ever affected, no matter what
options.outcome: If you reuse the password elsewhere, other accounts become at risk too, not just the one that was hacked.

slides.title: Be suspicious of “free” rewards
slides.text: “Free V-Bucks,” gift cards, rare skins, or giveaways that ask for your login are common bait. Real rewards should never require you to hand over your password.

widgetConfig.scenario: An ad offers "free V-Bucks" if you give your login. Should you trust this?

options.label: No — real rewards never require your password
options.outcome: Exactly right! "Free" rewards that ask for your login are common bait — real rewards should never require you to hand over your password.

options.label: Yes, giving your login for free rewards is always safe
options.outcome: Giving your login for a free reward is risky — real rewards never require your password.

options.label: Free reward offers are never a common scam tactic
options.outcome: Free reward offers that ask for logins are actually a very common scam tactic, worth being suspicious of.

slides.title: Know when game spending becomes real spending
slides.text: One-tap purchases, loot boxes, subscriptions, and upgrades can make real money feel like game points. Check the price and ask before buying or subscribing.

widgetConfig.scenario: A one-tap purchase in a game feels like just points. Is it actually free?

options.label: No — it can use real money
options.outcome: Exactly right! One-tap purchases, loot boxes, and upgrades can make real money feel like game points — check the price and ask before buying.

options.label: Yes, in-game purchases never cost real money
options.outcome: In-game purchases can actually cost real money, even when they feel like just points.

options.label: Only purchases outside apps ever use real money
options.outcome: Purchases inside apps and games can use real money too, not just purchases made outside them.

slides.title: Free trials can become paid subscriptions
slides.text: A “7-day free trial” may begin charging automatically on day 8. Before starting one, check the renewal price, cancellation date, and whether a card is required.

widgetConfig.scenario: A "7-day free trial" signs you up. What might happen on day 8?

options.label: It may start charging automatically
options.outcome: Exactly right! A '7-day free trial' may begin charging automatically on day 8 — check the renewal price and cancellation date before starting one.

options.label: It always stays free forever with no charges
options.outcome: Free trials don't always stay free forever — they often start charging automatically once the trial ends.

options.label: Free trials never actually lead to any charges
options.outcome: Free trials actually can lead to charges, once the trial period ends and renewal kicks in.

slides.title: Verify through a separate channel
slides.text: If a message seems unusual—even from a friend—check another way. For example, if a friend suddenly asks for money, call or message them somewhere else instead of trusting the same conversation.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend's account suddenly asks you for money. What should you do?

options.label: Call or message them a different way to check
options.outcome: Exactly right! If a message seems unusual, even from a friend, check another way — call or message them somewhere else instead of trusting the same conversation.

options.label: Send the money right away since it is a friend
options.outcome: Sending money right away is risky, since the account could be compromised — verifying through a separate channel is safer.

options.label: Unusual requests from friends’ accounts are never worth double-checking
options.outcome: Unusual requests are actually worth double-checking, even from a friend's account, since it could be compromised.

slides.title: If you clicked, act quickly
slides.text: Clicking a suspicious link does not mean everything is lost. Stop entering information, tell a trusted adult, change any password you typed, and review the account for unusual activity.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap what to do, in the right order
items: Review the account for unusual activity

slides.title: Scams can happen inside games
slides.text: Fake trades, “free skin” links, and people pretending to be game staff can all be scams. Real staff generally use official in-game or support systems, not random private login links.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone claiming to be game staff messages you privately asking to log in somewhere. Is this likely legitimate?

options.label: No — real staff use official in-game or support systems
options.outcome: Exactly right! Real game staff generally use official in-game or support systems, not random private login links — this is a common scam pattern.

options.label: Yes, private messages from “staff” are always legitimate
options.outcome: Private messages claiming to be from staff aren't always legitimate — real staff use official channels, not random private links.

options.label: Scams can never happen inside video games
options.outcome: Scams actually can happen inside games too, like fake trades or people pretending to be staff.

slides.title: Check the whole web address
slides.text: Fake sites often use look-alike spellings, extra words, or strange domains. Before signing in, check the address carefully and, when possible, open the official app or type the site yourself.

widgetConfig.scenario: A site looks like your favorite store but the web address looks slightly off. What should you do?

options.label: Check the address carefully or type the site yourself
options.outcome: Exactly right! Fake sites often use look-alike spellings or strange domains — check the address carefully, or open the official app or type the site yourself.

options.label: Sign in right away since it looks familiar
options.outcome: Signing in right away is risky if the address looks slightly off — checking it carefully is safer.

options.label: Web addresses never reveal whether a site is fake
options.outcome: Web addresses actually can reveal a fake site — checking them carefully for look-alike spellings matters.

quiz.question: An email looking like it's from a game company says "click here to verify your password or your account will be deleted." What is this?
choices: Phishing — a fake message trying to steal your info
A normal, safe security check
quiz.explanation: Phishing messages copy the look of a real company to pressure you into typing in your password or personal details. The fake urgency, like a countdown to account deletion, is designed to make you act before you think it through.

quiz.question: What does two-factor authentication add to an account?
choices: An extra security step beyond just a password
Nothing useful at all
quiz.explanation: Two-factor authentication adds a second lock beyond your password, usually a one-time code sent to your phone. Even if someone steals your password, they still can't get in without that second code, which only you receive.

quiz.question: Why is using a different password for every account safer than reusing one?
choices: One leak won't affect your other accounts
It makes passwords easier to guess
quiz.explanation: If you reuse one password everywhere and it leaks from one site, hackers can try that same password on your other accounts too. A unique password for each account keeps one leak from spreading to everything else you use.

quiz.question: A message says "enter your login to get free V-bucks." What is this?
choices: A scam trying to steal your password
A legitimate reward from the game company
quiz.explanation: Legitimate services should never require you to give a password to claim a reward — that's a classic bait used to steal passwords. Once scammers have your login, they can take over the account entirely.

quiz.question: A 'free trial' subscription auto-renews unless you act. What should you do if you don't want to keep paying?
choices: Cancel it before the trial period ends
Ignore it — trials never charge you
quiz.explanation: Free trials are designed to turn into paid subscriptions automatically once the trial period ends, unless you cancel first. A 'free for 7 days' game pass can quietly start charging a card every month after that week is up.

quiz.question: A text claiming to be from a friend urgently asks to borrow money. What's the safest move?
choices: Contact them a different, trusted way to confirm it's really them
Send the money right away since they said it's urgent
quiz.explanation: Scammers sometimes hack an account and message that person's real friends, pretending to be them in an emergency. Calling or texting the friend a different way confirms whether the urgent request is really from them.

quiz.question: You realize you just clicked a suspicious link. What should you do?
choices: Say nothing and hope nothing happens
Tell a trusted adult and change your password
quiz.explanation: Clicking one bad link doesn't automatically mean disaster, especially if you act fast. Telling a trusted adult and changing your password right away, instead of staying quiet, limits whatever damage might happen.

quiz.question: Someone in a game claims to be a 'moderator' and sends a login link. What is this most likely?
choices: A scam — real staff don't ask this way
A normal part of the game
quiz.explanation: Real game staff manage accounts through the game's own official systems, never by texting you a private login link. A stranger claiming to be a 'moderator' this way is almost always trying to steal your account.

quiz.question: A game offers 'buy now, decide later' one-click purchases saved to a card. Why is this worth extra caution?
choices: It can make spending real money feel less real
It has no relation to real money at all
quiz.explanation: When a purchase takes just one tap and the card is already saved, it can feel like nothing was really spent, even though real money left a real account. That's exactly why these purchases deserve extra caution.

quiz.question: An email link goes to 'arnazon.com' instead of 'amazon.com'. What does this small difference suggest?
choices: It's likely a fake, phishing website
It's just a normal typo that means nothing
quiz.explanation: Scammers register web addresses that look almost identical to a real one, hoping a quick glance won't catch the difference. Typing a password into a copycat site like 'arnazon.com' hands it straight to whoever built the fake page.

slides.title: Fake accounts and catfishing
slides.text: Someone online might use a fake photo and name to pretend to be someone they're not — this is sometimes called 'catfishing.' For example, an account claiming to be a 13-year-old with a cute profile photo could actually belong to a much older adult using a stolen or fake picture — which is why meeting an online-only friend in person always needs a trusted adult involved.

widgetConfig.scenario: An account claims to be a 13-year-old with a cute photo. Could this actually be an adult using a fake picture?

options.label: Yes — this is sometimes called catfishing
options.outcome: Exactly right! Someone online might use a fake photo and name to pretend to be someone they're not — this is sometimes called catfishing.

options.label: No, profile photos always prove who someone really is
options.outcome: Profile photos don't always prove who someone really is — they can be faked, which is why meeting online-only friends needs a trusted adult involved.

options.label: This never happens online
options.outcome: This actually does happen online, which is why caution and a trusted adult's involvement matter.

slides.title: When to disengage and report
slides.text: If an online conversation starts feeling uncomfortable or pressuring, stopping the conversation and reporting or telling a trusted adult is always okay. For example, if someone online keeps pushing you to share a photo or secret you don't want to share, ending the conversation and telling a trusted adult right away is the right call, no matter what they said to try to stop you.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone online keeps pushing you to share a photo you don't want to share. What should you do?

options.label: End the conversation and tell a trusted adult right away
options.outcome: Exactly right! If a conversation feels uncomfortable or pressuring, stopping it and telling a trusted adult is always okay, no matter what they said to try to stop you.

options.label: Keep talking until they stop asking
options.outcome: Continuing the conversation can mean more pressure — ending it and telling a trusted adult is the right call.

options.label: Stopping a conversation like this is never okay
options.outcome: Stopping a conversation like this is actually always okay — it's the right response to pressure like this.

slides.title: Location sharing risks
slides.text: Live location sharing can be useful with close family, but sharing it publicly or with people you barely know can reveal exactly where you are, in real time. For example, sharing your live location with a parent so they know you got to a friend's house safely makes sense, but sharing that same live location publicly means literally anyone could see exactly where you are right now.

widgetConfig.scenario: An app asks to share your real-time location publicly with everyone, not just friends. What should you do?

options.label: Turn off public location sharing — only trusted people should see it
options.outcome: Right — sharing your real-time location publicly can let strangers know exactly where you are, which is a real safety risk.

options.label: Leave it on since it's convenient
options.outcome: Public location sharing can let strangers track exactly where you are — it's safer to keep that information private.

options.label: Share it so you don't look rude
options.outcome: Your safety matters more than appearances — it's okay to keep your location private.

slides.title: Online friends vs. real friends
slides.text: Someone you've only ever talked to online is different from a friend you actually know in person — it's wise to be more cautious about what you share and trust. For example, an online gaming friend you've chatted with for months might seem trustworthy, but since you've never actually met them in person, it makes sense to be more careful about what personal details you share with them.

widgetConfig.scenario: You've chatted with an online gaming friend for months but never met in person. Should you treat them exactly like a friend you know in person?

options.label: No — it is wise to be more cautious about what you share
options.outcome: Exactly right! Someone you've only ever talked to online is different from a friend you actually know — it's wise to be more cautious about what you share and trust.

options.label: Yes, treat them exactly the same as someone you have met
options.outcome: Treating an online-only friend exactly like someone you've met in person skips important caution about what you share.

options.label: How long you have chatted online always proves real trust
options.outcome: The length of time chatting online doesn't automatically prove real trust — caution is still wise.

slides.title: Warning signs in online friendships
slides.text: An online contact who asks you to keep the friendship secret from your parents, or who gets upset when you don't reply instantly, is showing warning signs worth paying attention to. For example, someone who says 'don't tell your parents about our chats' is using a tactic real friends and trustworthy adults never need to use.

widgetConfig.scenario: An online contact asks you to keep your friendship secret from your parents. What should you do?

options.label: See it as a warning sign and tell a trusted adult
options.outcome: Exactly right! Asking you to keep secrets from your parents is a major warning sign — telling a trusted adult is the safe move.

options.label: Keep it secret since they asked nicely
options.outcome: Being asked to keep something secret from your parents is a warning sign, no matter how it's asked — tell a trusted adult.

options.label: It's normal for online friends to ask for secrecy
options.outcome: It's not normal — asking for secrecy from your parents is a red flag worth telling a trusted adult about.

slides.title: Profile pictures can be stolen
slides.text: A profile photo can be copied from someone else's real account and reused to create a fake, convincing profile. For example, running a suspicious profile picture through a reverse image search can sometimes reveal it actually belongs to someone else entirely.

widgetConfig.scenario: A reverse image search shows a profile photo actually belongs to someone else. What does this reveal?

options.label: The profile could be fake, using a stolen photo
options.outcome: Exactly right! A profile photo can be copied from someone else's real account and reused to create a fake, convincing profile.

options.label: Nothing — profile photos can never be reused by others
options.outcome: Profile photos actually can be reused by others — that's exactly what a reverse image search can reveal.

options.label: This proves the account is definitely trustworthy
options.outcome: This actually suggests the opposite — a stolen photo is a sign the profile could be fake, not trustworthy.

slides.title: Gifts and favors with strings attached
slides.text: Someone online offering gifts, game currency, or special attention may be trying to build trust before asking for something in return. For example, a stranger who generously gifts rare in-game items before asking for personal photos or information is following a well-known manipulation pattern.

widgetConfig.scenario: An online friend offers to buy you expensive game currency, but says to keep it a secret from your parents. What's the red flag here?

options.label: Asking you to keep secrets from trusted adults is a major warning sign
options.outcome: Exactly right — anyone asking you to hide something from your parents, especially tied to a gift, is a serious red flag.

options.label: It's totally fine since it's just a nice gift
options.outcome: A generous gift tied to secrecy is a classic manipulation tactic — the secrecy part is the red flag, not the gift itself.

options.label: Accept it but don't use it
options.outcome: Even accepting it can create pressure to repay the favor — it's safer to tell a trusted adult about the offer.

slides.title: Why trusted adults, not secrecy, keep you safest
slides.text: Keeping a trusted adult in the loop about online relationships isn't about losing privacy — it's about having backup if something feels wrong. For example, telling a parent 'I made a new friend in this game' before anything feels off means they already have context if something does go wrong later.

widgetConfig.scenario: You tell a parent "I made a new friend in this game" before anything feels off. Why does this help?

options.label: They already have context if something goes wrong later
options.outcome: Exactly right! Keeping a trusted adult in the loop isn't about losing privacy — it means they already have context if something does go wrong later.

options.label: It makes no difference either way
options.outcome: It actually makes a real difference — a trusted adult having context ahead of time helps if something goes wrong later.

options.label: Telling a trusted adult early is always unnecessary
options.outcome: Telling a trusted adult early is actually a smart habit, giving them helpful context if something feels wrong later.

slides.title: Trusting your gut feeling
slides.text: If an interaction online feels off, even if you can't explain exactly why, that instinct is worth listening to and acting on. For example, feeling uneasy about a conversation's turn, even without a specific 'red flag,' is a good enough reason to step back and tell someone.

widgetConfig.scenario: A conversation online feels off, even though you can't explain exactly why. What should you do?

options.label: Listen to that instinct and step back
options.outcome: Exactly right! If an interaction feels off, even without a specific 'red flag,' that instinct is worth listening to and acting on.

options.label: Ignore the feeling since you cannot explain it
options.outcome: Ignoring a gut feeling skips useful information — it's worth listening to even without a specific explanation.

options.label: A feeling without a specific reason is never worth acting on
options.outcome: A gut feeling is actually worth acting on, even without a specific, nameable reason.

quiz.question: An account claims to be a 13-year-old but might actually be a much older adult using a fake photo. What is this called?
choices: Catfishing — pretending to be someone else online
A type of fishing you do with a net
quiz.explanation: Catfishing is when someone builds a fake identity online, often using a stolen photo and a made-up age or name, to trick people into trusting them. A profile claiming to be 13 could actually belong to an adult using someone else's picture.

quiz.question: Someone online keeps pressuring you to share a photo you don't want to share. What should you do?
choices: Stop the conversation and tell a trusted adult
Keep going no matter how it feels
quiz.explanation: Real friends don't keep pushing after you say no, so repeated pressure is itself a warning sign. Ending the conversation and telling a trusted adult is the right move, regardless of what the person says to stop you.

quiz.question: Why can public live location sharing be riskier than sharing it just with a parent?
choices: It can reveal exactly where you are, in real time, to people you barely know
It has no risk in any situation
quiz.explanation: Sharing your live location with a parent lets them check you arrived somewhere safely. Sharing that same live location publicly means anyone, including strangers, could watch exactly where you are in real time.

quiz.question: Should you trust an online-only gaming friend the same as someone you know in person?
choices: It's wise to be more cautious
Yes, trust them exactly the same amount
quiz.explanation: Someone you've only met through a screen could be exactly who they claim, or could be presenting a made-up identity — there's no way to fully check. That uncertainty is why sharing personal details with online-only contacts deserves more caution.

quiz.question: An online contact says "don't tell your parents about our chats." What does this suggest?
choices: A warning sign worth paying attention to
A completely normal request from a friend
quiz.explanation: Asking someone to hide a friendship from their parents is a common tactic used to isolate a person from people who'd otherwise notice something wrong. Trustworthy adults and real friends never need secrecy to justify a relationship.

quiz.question: What can a reverse image search sometimes reveal about a suspicious profile picture?
choices: That it was actually copied from someone else's real account
Nothing useful — image searches don't work that way
quiz.explanation: A reverse image search compares a photo against others already online to find where it originally came from. If a 'new' profile picture turns out to belong to someone else's years-old real account, that's a strong sign of a fake profile.

quiz.question: A stranger online gives you rare, generous gifts before asking for personal photos. What is this pattern?
choices: A well-known manipulation tactic to build trust first
Just a kind, generous stranger with no motive
quiz.explanation: Offering generous gifts before making a request is a manipulation technique that builds a feeling of trust or obligation first. That's exactly why unusually generous strangers online are worth extra suspicion.

quiz.question: Why does telling a trusted adult about a new online friend help, even if nothing seems wrong yet?
choices: It only matters after something bad happens
They already have context if something goes wrong later
quiz.explanation: Mentioning a new online friend to a parent before anything feels off means they already have the full picture if a problem shows up later. Waiting until something feels wrong makes it harder to explain everything at once.

quiz.question: You feel uneasy about a conversation but can't explain exactly why. What should you do?
choices: Trust that feeling and step back or tell someone
Ignore it since you can't name a specific reason
quiz.explanation: Feelings of unease often notice small warning signs before your conscious mind can name exactly what's wrong. Stepping back or telling someone, even without a specific reason, is a smart, reasonable response.

quiz.question: Someone's profile claims one age but their photos and writing style seem to suggest otherwise. What should you consider?
choices: The profile might not be what it claims to be
Profiles are always exactly as they describe themselves
quiz.explanation: When small details about a profile don't add up, like photos that look older than the stated age, it's a sign the profile might not be genuine. Trusting your own observation over the stated claim is reasonable caution.

slides.title: Oversharing online
slides.text: Posting your location, school name, or daily schedule can reveal more about you to strangers than you might realize. For example, a post saying "at soccer practice every Tuesday at 4pm at Central Park" tells any stranger exactly where to find you at a specific, predictable time — far more than most people would say out loud to someone they don't know.

widgetConfig.scenario: You post "at soccer practice every Tuesday at 4pm at Central Park." What does this reveal to strangers?

options.label: Exactly where to find you at a predictable time
options.outcome: Exactly right! A post like this tells any stranger exactly where to find you at a specific, predictable time — far more than most people would say out loud to a stranger.

options.label: Nothing useful to anyone
options.outcome: This post actually reveals something quite useful to a stranger — exactly where and when to find you.

options.label: Posting specific routines never reveals anything risky
options.outcome: Posting specific routines like this actually can reveal real risk, showing exactly where to find you.

slides.title: Your digital footprint
slides.text: Everything you post, like, or comment online adds up over time into a 'digital footprint' — a trail that can be seen by others, even years later. For example, comments and photos posted at age 12 can still be found by someone searching your name years later, which is why it's worth thinking about before posting.

widgetConfig.scenario: Everything you post, like, or comment online adds up over time. What is this collection called?

options.label: Your digital footprint
options.outcome: Exactly right! Everything you post, like, or comment adds up over time into what's called your digital footprint.

options.label: Your Wi-Fi signal
options.outcome: That's unrelated to your online activity — the record of everything you post and like is called your digital footprint.

options.label: It doesn't add up to anything meaningful
options.outcome: It actually does add up — this ongoing record is called your digital footprint, and it can matter a lot.

slides.title: Group chats and screenshots
slides.text: Anything sent in a group chat can be screenshotted and shared far beyond the people it was meant for, even if it felt private at the time. For example, a joke or complaint sent to one friend in a group chat could be screenshotted and shared with people who were never meant to see it, which is worth remembering before hitting send.

widgetConfig.scenario: You send a complaint about a friend in a group chat. Could it be seen by people beyond the group?

options.label: Yes — it could be screenshotted and shared further
options.outcome: Exactly right! Anything sent in a group chat can be screenshotted and shared far beyond the people it was meant for, even if it felt private at the time.

options.label: No, group chats always stay completely private
options.outcome: Group chats don't always stay completely private — messages can be screenshotted and shared beyond the group.

options.label: Screenshots are never possible in a group chat
options.outcome: Screenshots are actually always possible in a group chat, which is worth remembering before hitting send.

slides.title: Balancing screen time
slides.text: Noticing when screen time is crowding out sleep, friends, or activities you enjoy is an important digital safety and wellbeing skill. For example, if staying up late scrolling means you're too tired to enjoy soccer practice the next day, that's a sign screen time might need rebalancing.

widgetConfig.scenario: Staying up late scrolling makes you too tired to enjoy soccer practice. What does this suggest?

options.label: Screen time might need rebalancing
options.outcome: Exactly right! Noticing when screen time is crowding out sleep or activities you enjoy is a sign it might need rebalancing.

options.label: Nothing — tiredness never relates to screen time
options.outcome: Tiredness actually can relate directly to screen time, like staying up late scrolling before an activity.

options.label: This is a sign you should scroll even more
options.outcome: Feeling too tired to enjoy an activity is a signal to rebalance screen time, not to scroll even more.

slides.title: Anyone can search your name
slides.text: Typing your own name into a search engine occasionally, sometimes called a 'self-search,' shows you what strangers, teachers, or future coaches might already find. For example, discovering an old public post you forgot about is a useful nudge to check your privacy settings or delete it.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're thinking about what to post online. Someone mentions that anyone could search your name and find it later. What should you consider?

options.label: Think about whether you'd be okay with anyone, including future employers, seeing it
options.outcome: Great awareness! Since anyone can search your name, it's smart to think about how something might look to people beyond just your friends.

options.label: It doesn't matter since only friends will see it
options.outcome: Posts can often be found by searching your name, even by people outside your friend circle — it's worth thinking about the wider audience.

options.label: Nothing posted online can ever be found later
options.outcome: Actually, a lot of what's posted online can be searched and found later — it's worth considering that before posting.

slides.title: Tags and check-ins add up too
slides.text: Being tagged in a friend's post, or checking in at a location, can share information about you even when you didn't post anything yourself. For example, a friend tagging you at a specific restaurant reveals where you are, even if your own account is completely private.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend tags you at a specific restaurant. Does this reveal your location even if your own account is private?

options.label: Yes — tags can reveal your location regardless
options.outcome: Exactly right! Being tagged in a friend's post can share information about you, even if your own account is completely private.

options.label: No, only your own posts can ever reveal where you are
options.outcome: Your own posts aren't the only way — a friend tagging you can reveal your location too, even with a private account.

options.label: Being tagged by someone else never shares any information
options.outcome: Being tagged by someone else actually can share real information about you, like your location.

slides.title: Deleting doesn't always mean gone
slides.text: Deleting a post removes it from your profile, but people may have already seen, saved, or screenshotted it before it was deleted. For example, a post deleted five minutes after posting can still exist as a screenshot on someone else's phone.

widgetConfig.scenario: You post something online, then delete it a minute later because you regret it. Is it definitely gone for good?

options.label: Not necessarily — others may have already seen or screenshotted it
options.outcome: Right — once something is posted, even briefly, it can be captured before you delete it. That's why it's smart to think before posting, not just after.

options.label: Yes, deleting always removes it completely everywhere
options.outcome: Deleting removes it from your own page, but screenshots or saves made before deletion can still exist.

options.label: It doesn't matter since no one saw it that fast
options.outcome: Even a short window is enough for someone to screenshot something — it's safest to think before posting.

slides.title: Noticing screen time patterns, not just totals
slides.text: Paying attention to when and why you reach for a screen, like out of boredom or after an upsetting moment, reveals more than just counting total hours. For example, noticing you always open an app right after feeling left out is useful information about the habit, not just the time spent.

widgetConfig.scenario: You notice you always open an app right after feeling left out. What's useful about noticing this?

options.label: It reveals something about the habit, not just the time spent
options.outcome: Exactly right! Paying attention to when and why you reach for a screen reveals more than just counting total hours.

options.label: Nothing — only the total hours matter
options.outcome: Total hours aren't the only useful thing — noticing the 'why' behind reaching for a screen reveals more.

options.label: Noticing when and why you use a screen is never useful
options.outcome: Noticing when and why you use a screen is actually quite useful — it's more informative than just totals.

slides.title: Setting your own healthy limits
slides.text: Deciding in advance on limits, like no phones at the dinner table or an hour before bed, makes healthy screen habits easier to stick to in the moment. For example, agreeing on a charging spot outside the bedroom overnight is a simple rule that helps sleep without needing willpower every night.

widgetConfig.scenario: You agree on a charging spot outside the bedroom overnight. What does this help with?

options.label: Sticking to healthy screen habits without needing willpower every night
