options.outcome: Exactly right! Deciding on limits in advance, like a charging spot outside the bedroom, makes healthy screen habits easier to stick to without needing willpower every night.

options.label: Nothing — limits set in advance never actually help
options.outcome: Limits set in advance actually help a lot — they make good habits easier to stick to without needing willpower each night.

options.label: This makes screen habits harder to maintain
options.outcome: This kind of advance rule actually makes healthy screen habits easier to maintain, not harder.

quiz.question: What is a "digital footprint"?
choices: The trail your posts, likes, and comments leave over time
A picture of your actual foot
quiz.explanation: Every post, like, and comment you make online adds up into a lasting trail called your 'digital footprint.' Even something posted years ago, like a comment at age 10, can still be found by someone searching your name later.

quiz.question: A post says "at soccer practice every Tuesday at 4pm at Central Park." Why might that be risky?
choices: It can reveal more to strangers than intended
It has no effect on your safety at all
quiz.explanation: Posting a specific time and place, like practice every Tuesday at 4pm, tells any stranger exactly where to find you and when. Most people wouldn't say that out loud to someone they don't know, so it's worth the same caution online.

quiz.question: Can something sent in a "private" group chat still be shared with others?
choices: Yes, it can be screenshotted and shared further
No, group chats are always completely private
quiz.explanation: A group chat can feel private in the moment, but anyone in it can take a screenshot and send it somewhere else entirely. A joke meant for one friend could end up seen by people who were never supposed to see it.

quiz.question: What does occasionally searching your own name online help you notice?
choices: What strangers or future coaches might already find about you
Nothing useful — self-searching has no purpose
quiz.explanation: Searching your own name occasionally shows you the same things a stranger, teacher, or future coach might find. Spotting an old, forgotten public post this way gives you the chance to delete it or fix your privacy settings.

quiz.question: A friend tags you at a restaurant even though your own account is private. What happens?
choices: Your location info can still be shared through their tag
Nothing — private accounts block all tags completely
quiz.explanation: A private account only controls what you post yourself, not what other people post about you. A friend's tag or check-in can still reveal your location, even if your own profile is completely locked down.

quiz.question: You delete a post five minutes after posting it. Is it definitely gone for good?
choices: Not necessarily — someone may have already screenshotted it
Yes, deleting always removes every trace instantly
quiz.explanation: Deleting a post removes it from your own profile, but it doesn't erase copies other people may have already saved or screenshotted. Something seen even briefly can end up saved forever on someone else's phone.

quiz.question: Noticing you always open an app right after feeling left out is an example of what?
choices: Something that has nothing to do with screen habits
Paying attention to screen time patterns, not just totals
quiz.explanation: Noticing the moment you reach for a screen, like right after feeling left out, reveals more about the habit than just counting total hours would. That pattern points to why you're scrolling, not just how much.

quiz.question: Setting a rule like "no phones at the dinner table" in advance helps because...
choices: It removes the need for willpower in the moment
Rules made in advance never actually help
quiz.explanation: Deciding a rule ahead of time, like no phones at dinner, means you don't have to make that decision in the moment when a notification is tempting you. Planning removes the need for willpower right when it's hardest.

quiz.question: A public post says "home alone until 6pm today." Why is this risky?
choices: It reveals when your home might be empty, to anyone who sees it
It has no real-world risk at all
quiz.explanation: A post announcing you're home alone, and for how long, tells anyone who sees it exactly when your house might be empty. That's information most people would never say out loud to a stranger.

quiz.question: Posting your daily school pickup time and location publicly is risky mainly because...
choices: It reveals a predictable pattern of where you'll be
Predictable patterns online are never a concern
quiz.explanation: Posting the same pickup time and place every day creates a predictable pattern that a stranger could use to know exactly where you'll be. Routines shared publicly are riskier than one-time posts precisely because they repeat.

slides.title: Social engineering
slides.text: Social engineering targets people rather than computers. Scammers use urgency, fear, authority, or trust—such as “verify in 10 minutes or lose your account”—to push you into acting before you think.

widgetConfig.scenario: A message creates urgency and fear to trick you into acting fast, targeting you rather than a computer system. What is this called?

options.label: Social engineering
options.outcome: Exactly right! Social engineering targets people rather than computers, using urgency and fear to trick someone into acting fast.

options.label: A software bug
options.outcome: A software bug is a technical flaw in code — tricking a person using urgency and fear is called social engineering.

options.label: A firewall
options.outcome: A firewall is a security tool that protects systems — tricking a person this way is called social engineering.

slides.title: Deepfakes and misinformation
slides.text: AI can create convincing fake images, voices, and video. If a clip is shocking or important, check whether reliable sources and the original account confirm it before believing or sharing it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A shocking video clip is circulating online. What should you do before believing or sharing it?

options.label: Check whether reliable sources confirm it
options.outcome: Exactly right! AI can create convincing fake images, voices, and video — check whether reliable sources and the original account confirm it before believing or sharing.

options.label: Share it immediately since it looks real
options.outcome: Sharing immediately risks spreading a convincing fake — checking reliable sources first is safer.

options.label: AI can never create convincing fake video
options.outcome: AI actually can create very convincing fake video and images, which is why checking sources matters.

slides.title: Public Wi-Fi: understand the real risk
slides.text: Modern encrypted apps and HTTPS protect much of your traffic, but public Wi-Fi can still be risky through fake networks, malicious redirects, or poor device security. Avoid sensitive tasks on networks you do not trust, and use cellular data or a trusted network when practical.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're at a coffee shop and want to check your bank account using the public Wi-Fi. What's the safer approach?

options.label: Use cellular data or a VPN instead of public Wi-Fi for sensitive stuff
options.outcome: Good call — public Wi-Fi can be less secure for sensitive activities like banking, so using cellular data or a VPN adds real protection.

options.label: Public Wi-Fi is totally fine for anything
options.outcome: Public Wi-Fi carries more risk for sensitive activities like banking — it's safer to avoid it for that or use added protection.

options.label: Avoid using the internet at all while out
options.outcome: You don't need to avoid the internet entirely — just be more careful about which networks you use for sensitive things like banking.

slides.title: Protecting financial information online
slides.text: Do not enter card or banking details from a surprise text, DM, or email link. Open the official app or type the company’s known website yourself; a padlock/HTTPS protects the connection but does not prove the business itself is legitimate.

widgetConfig.scenario: A surprise text link asks for your card details. What's the safer approach?

options.label: Open the official app or type the website yourself
options.outcome: Exactly right! Do not enter card or banking details from a surprise text, DM, or email link — open the official app or type the company's known website yourself.

options.label: Enter your card details right through the link
options.outcome: Entering details through a surprise link is risky — opening the official app or typing the website yourself is much safer.

options.label: A padlock/HTTPS icon alone proves a business is legitimate
options.outcome: A padlock or HTTPS protects the connection, but it doesn't prove the business itself is legitimate.

slides.title: Scams aimed at teens
slides.text: Fake jobs, “easy money,” fake scholarships, romance scams, and payment requests all target teens. A job that requires you to pay a fee, buy gift cards, or send money before you are hired is a major warning sign.

widgetConfig.scenario: You see a "job offer" online promising easy money for just a few minutes of work a day, no experience needed. What's the smartest response?

options.label: Research the company and be skeptical of guarantees
options.outcome: Good instinct — "easy money, no experience" offers are a common scam pattern aimed at teens looking for quick income.

options.label: Sign up immediately and provide bank details
options.outcome: Scams targeting teens often ask for bank or payment info upfront — that's a major red flag, not a real job requirement.

options.label: Share the "opportunity" with friends so they can join too
options.outcome: Spreading the offer to friends can pull them into the same scam — better to verify it first.

slides.title: Check whether old credentials were exposed
slides.text: A company breach can expose old usernames, emails, or passwords. If you learn that one of your passwords was exposed, change it anywhere it was reused and turn on 2FA.

widgetConfig.scenario: You learn one of your passwords was exposed in a company breach. What should you do?

options.label: Change it anywhere it was reused and turn on 2FA
options.outcome: Exactly right! If a password was exposed, change it anywhere it was reused and turn on 2FA.

options.label: Ignore it since the breach was not your fault
options.outcome: Even though a breach isn't your fault, ignoring an exposed password leaves your accounts at risk — changing it protects you.

options.label: An exposed password never needs to be changed
options.outcome: An exposed password actually does need to be changed, especially anywhere it was reused.

slides.title: Spear phishing uses details about you
slides.text: A targeted scam may mention your school, employer, coach, or friend to look believable. Real details do not prove the message is real—verify sensitive requests independently.

widgetConfig.scenario: A scam message mentions your real school and coach's name. Does this prove the message is legitimate?

options.label: No — real details do not prove a message is real
options.outcome: Exactly right! A targeted scam may mention real details like your school or coach to look believable — real details don't prove the message is real.

options.label: Yes, knowing real details always means it is legitimate
options.outcome: Knowing real details doesn't prove legitimacy — scammers can gather real details to look more convincing.

options.label: Scams never use real personal details to seem believable
options.outcome: Scams actually do use real personal details on purpose, to look more believable — that's exactly what spear phishing is.

slides.title: Fake checkout pages can look polished
slides.text: Scam stores may copy real logos and product photos. Warning signs include a look-alike domain, unrealistic prices, poor contact information, pressure to pay quickly, or unusual payment methods.

widgetConfig.scenario: An online store has a web address that's almost identical to a real brand's name, with one letter different. Is this a warning sign?

options.label: Yes — a look-alike domain is a classic scam warning sign
options.outcome: Exactly! Scam stores often copy real logos and photos but give themselves away with a look-alike domain name.

options.label: No, a polished-looking site is always trustworthy
options.outcome: A polished look doesn't guarantee safety — scam sites can copy real branding closely, so checking the domain matters.

options.label: Only the price matters, not the web address
options.outcome: The web address matters a lot — a look-alike domain is one of the clearest scam warning signs.

slides.title: If money or credentials were stolen, act fast
slides.text: Tell a trusted adult, change affected passwords, and contact the bank/card provider if money was involved. Quick reporting can limit further charges or account takeovers.

widgetConfig.scenario: You realize your account and some money may have been stolen. What should you do?

options.label: Tell a trusted adult, change passwords, contact the provider
options.outcome: Exactly right! Tell a trusted adult, change affected passwords, and contact the bank or card provider — quick reporting can limit further charges.

options.label: Wait a while before telling anyone
options.outcome: Waiting can let the problem get worse — quick reporting can limit further charges or account takeovers.

options.label: Quick reporting never actually limits further damage
options.outcome: Quick reporting actually can limit further damage, like additional charges or account takeovers.

quiz.question: A message says "your account will be locked in 10 minutes unless you verify now." What tactic is this?
choices: Social engineering — using manufactured urgency to pressure you
A normal, harmless account notice
quiz.explanation: Social engineering is manipulating someone's emotions, like fear or urgency, to get them to act before thinking it through, rather than hacking a computer directly. A countdown threatening account deletion is a manufactured deadline meant to short-circuit your judgment.

quiz.question: Why are deepfakes concerning for digital safety?
choices: They can convincingly fake images, video, or audio
They are always obviously fake and harmless
quiz.explanation: A deepfake uses AI to generate fake video, audio, or images realistic enough to show someone saying or doing something that never actually happened. Verifying a shocking claim against a trusted news source before believing or sharing it has become an essential habit.

quiz.question: Why is logging into a banking app on free coffee-shop Wi-Fi risky?
choices: Others on the same network could potentially access your data
Public Wi-Fi is always perfectly safe for anything
quiz.explanation: Public Wi-Fi is shared with strangers and can include fake or poorly secured networks. Modern encrypted apps protect much of your traffic, but sensitive tasks are still safer on a trusted network or cellular connection.

quiz.question: A text says "your package couldn't be delivered, click here and enter your card info." What should you do?
choices: Treat it as a likely scam and never enter card details through it
Enter your card info right away to fix the delivery
quiz.explanation: Legitimate delivery problems get resolved through the courier's official app or website, never by entering card details through a random text link. This pattern, an urgent problem paired with a surprise payment request, is one of the most common scam formats.

quiz.question: A message offers "$500 a week for easy work" if you pay a small fee first. What is this?
choices: A likely scam — real jobs don't charge you to get hired
A normal, trustworthy job offer
quiz.explanation: A real employer pays you for work — it never asks you to pay money upfront just to get hired. Offers promising easy money in exchange for an initial fee are a well-known scam pattern designed to take that fee and disappear.

quiz.question: An email references your actual part-time job by name before asking you to confirm payroll details. What makes this more dangerous than a generic scam email?
choices: It uses real details about you to seem convincing (spear phishing)
Nothing — personal details always mean a message is safe
quiz.explanation: Spear phishing uses real, specific details about a target, like their actual employer's name, to seem far more credible than a generic scam email. Referencing your real part-time job before asking you to 'confirm payroll info' is a targeted attempt built just for you.

quiz.question: A shopping site sells $180 sneakers for $19.99 and only accepts cryptocurrency. What does this suggest?
choices: A likely scam site, not a real deal
A trustworthy, generous sale
quiz.explanation: A price far below a product's normal value, combined with unusual payment demands like cryptocurrency only, is a well-known pattern for fake shopping sites. Real retailers rarely sell name-brand items at a steep, unexplained discount while refusing standard payment methods.

quiz.question: You realize you've just been scammed out of money. What should you do first?
choices: Stay quiet out of embarrassment
Tell a trusted adult and contact your bank quickly
quiz.explanation: Acting within minutes or hours, by telling a trusted adult and contacting the bank, gives the best chance of reversing a fraudulent charge before the money is gone for good. Staying silent out of embarrassment only gives a scammer more time to spend what they took.

quiz.question: Why does checking if your data has been breached matter, even if nothing seems wrong?
choices: A password could be exposed and reused elsewhere without you knowing
Data breaches never actually affect regular people
quiz.explanation: A data breach happens when a company's stored information, like usernames and passwords, is stolen by hackers, often without the company or its users noticing right away. If an old password was breached and reused elsewhere, every account sharing it is quietly exposed too.

quiz.question: What's a quick way to check if a shopping website might be fake?
choices: Look for a mismatched URL, missing https padlock, or unrealistic prices
Trust it automatically if the logo looks right
quiz.explanation: A mismatched web address, a strange web address, unrealistic prices, weak contact information, or unusual payment demands can all signal a fake shopping site. A padlock/HTTPS means the connection is encrypted, but scam sites can use HTTPS too, so also check the domain, price, contact information, and payment method.

slides.title: Password managers
slides.text: A password manager securely stores unique, complex passwords for every account, so you don't have to reuse the same weak password everywhere. For example, instead of using the same password for your email, social media, and school account (so one leak compromises everything), a password manager can generate and remember a different strong password for each one.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're tired of reusing the same password everywhere because it's hard to remember many different ones. What's a smart solution?

options.label: Use a password manager to generate and store unique passwords
options.outcome: Great solution! A password manager lets you have strong, unique passwords for every account without needing to memorize them all.

options.label: Keep reusing the same password everywhere
options.outcome: Reusing passwords means if one account is breached, all your accounts become vulnerable — unique passwords are much safer.

options.label: Write all your passwords on a sticky note
options.outcome: A password manager is a much safer way to handle many unique passwords than writing them down somewhere visible.

slides.title: Reading privacy policies (a little)
slides.text: You don't need to read every word, but understanding roughly what data an app collects and how it's used is a genuinely useful digital literacy skill. For example, noticing that an app's privacy policy says it shares your location data with advertisers might change whether you're comfortable granting it that permission.

widgetConfig.scenario: An app has a long privacy policy nobody reads. Is it worth understanding roughly what it says?

options.label: Yes — understanding roughly what data it collects is worth knowing
options.outcome: Exactly! You don't need to read every word, but understanding roughly what data an app collects is worth it.

options.label: No, privacy policies never contain useful information
options.outcome: Privacy policies actually do contain useful information about what data is collected, even in a quick skim.

options.label: Only lawyers need to ever think about privacy policies
options.outcome: Anyone using an app benefits from roughly understanding its privacy policy, not just lawyers.

slides.title: Recognizing predatory behavior
slides.text: Adults who push a minor toward secrecy, isolation from friends/family, or private communication are showing classic warning signs — reporting and telling a trusted adult matters. For example, an adult online who says "let's keep this conversation between just us" or discourages you from telling a parent is showing a well-documented warning sign that should be reported immediately.

widgetConfig.scenario: An adult online says "let's keep this conversation between just us." What does this show?

options.label: A well-documented warning sign that should be reported
options.outcome: Exactly right! Adults who push a minor toward secrecy or isolation are showing classic warning signs — reporting and telling a trusted adult matters.

slides.title: Location metadata in photos
slides.text: Photos taken on a phone often secretly store the exact location where they were taken, hidden inside the file itself as 'metadata.' For example, posting a photo taken at home, without realizing that many platforms or viewers can extract that embedded location data, could reveal exactly where you live to anyone who knows how to look for it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A photo taken at home contains hidden location data. Could this reveal where you live?

options.label: Yes — platforms or viewers can sometimes extract that data
options.outcome: Exactly right! Photos often secretly store the exact location where they were taken, hidden inside the file as metadata, which can reveal where you live.

options.label: No, photos never contain any hidden location information
options.outcome: Photos actually can contain hidden location data, called metadata, embedded inside the file.

options.label: Only the visible background of a photo can ever reveal location
options.outcome: Hidden metadata inside a photo file can reveal location too, not just what's visible in the background.

slides.title: Passphrases: long beats complicated
slides.text: A long string of random words, like 'correct-horse-battery-staple,' can actually be harder to crack than a short complex password, while being easier to remember. For example, security experts increasingly recommend passphrases of four or more unrelated words over short passwords stuffed with symbols that are hard to remember and often reused.

widgetConfig.scenario: Which tends to be harder to crack while still being easy to remember?

options.label: A long string of random words, like a passphrase
options.outcome: Exactly right! A long string of random words, like 'correct-horse-battery-staple,' can be harder to crack than a short complex password, while being easier to remember.

options.label: A short password stuffed with symbols
options.outcome: A short password stuffed with symbols is often harder to remember and not necessarily more secure than a long passphrase.

options.label: Length never affects how hard a password is to crack
options.outcome: Length actually affects this a lot — longer passphrases tend to be harder to crack than short complex ones.

slides.title: Grooming tactics, named clearly
slides.text: Predatory adults often follow a recognizable pattern: excessive flattery, gradually normalizing inappropriate topics, and testing boundaries with small requests before bigger ones. For example, an adult who starts with compliments, then slowly shifts to secretive or sexual topics over weeks, is following a well-documented grooming pattern — and it's never the target's fault.

widgetConfig.scenario: An adult starts with compliments, then slowly shifts to secretive topics over weeks. What does this pattern show?

options.label: A well-documented grooming pattern, and it is never the target's fault
options.outcome: Exactly right! Predatory adults often follow a recognizable pattern — excessive flattery, then gradually normalizing inappropriate topics — and it's never the target's fault.

options.label: Normal friendship behavior with no cause for concern
options.outcome: This isn't normal friendship behavior — this gradual shift is a well-documented grooming pattern worth reporting.

options.label: This kind of gradual pattern never actually happens
options.outcome: This kind of gradual pattern actually does happen and is well-documented, which is why it's named clearly for recognition.

slides.title: It's never too late to tell someone
slides.text: Even if an uncomfortable online relationship has been going on for a while, or you feel like you 'let it happen,' telling a trusted adult is always the right move, at any point. For example, a teen who shared photos months ago and feels it's 'too late' to say anything still deserves support, not judgment, for speaking up now.

widgetConfig.scenario: Something happened online months ago that made you uncomfortable, and you never told anyone. Is it too late to say something now?

options.label: No — it's never too late to tell a trusted adult

options.label: Yes, too much time has passed to say anything
options.outcome: It's genuinely never too late — trusted adults can still help, even if it happened a while ago.

options.label: Only if it happens again
options.outcome: You don't need to wait for it to happen again — telling someone now is still valuable and can prevent it from happening to you or others.

slides.title: Metadata beyond just photos
slides.text: Location metadata isn't limited to photos — check-ins, timestamps on posts, and even background details in a video can reveal where you are. For example, a video posted from a recognizable street sign or storefront can reveal your location just as clearly as GPS data embedded in a photo file.

widgetConfig.scenario: A video shows a recognizable street sign or storefront. Could this reveal your location, even without GPS data?

options.label: Yes — visible details in a video can reveal location too
options.outcome: Exactly right! Location metadata isn't limited to photos — visible background details in a video can reveal where you are, just as clearly as GPS data.

options.label: No, only GPS data embedded in photos ever reveals location
options.outcome: GPS data isn't the only way — visible details in a video, like a street sign, can reveal location too.

options.label: Videos can never reveal location information
options.outcome: Videos actually can reveal location information, through visible background details like signs or storefronts.

slides.title: What privacy settings can't fix
slides.text: Strong privacy settings limit who sees your content, but they don't stop a trusted follower from screenshotting and sharing it elsewhere. For example, even a fully private, followers-only account can't guarantee a post never leaves that circle once someone else has seen it.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your account is fully private, followers-only. Does this guarantee a post can never leave that circle?

options.label: No — a trusted follower could still screenshot and share it
options.outcome: Exactly right! Strong privacy settings limit who sees your content, but they don't stop a trusted follower from screenshotting and sharing it elsewhere.

options.label: Yes, private settings make sharing further completely impossible
options.outcome: Private settings don't make further sharing impossible — a trusted follower could still screenshot and share what they saw.

options.label: Privacy settings make screenshots impossible
options.outcome: Privacy settings actually can't prevent screenshots — a follower who can see your content can still screenshot it.

quiz.question: Why is reusing the same password across email, social media, and school accounts risky?
choices: One leak could compromise all of them at once
It makes each account more secure
quiz.explanation: When one site suffers a data breach and your password leaks, anyone with that password can try it on your other accounts too. A password manager, software that generates and remembers a unique strong password for every account, removes the need to reuse one at all.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to roughly understand an app's privacy policy?
choices: It helps you know what data is collected and how it's used
Privacy policies never contain any useful information
quiz.explanation: A privacy policy explains what data an app collects and who it's shared with, even if the full legal document is long and dense. Noticing a line about sharing your location with advertisers, for example, can change whether you're comfortable granting that permission.

quiz.question: An adult online says "let's keep this conversation between just us." What is this a sign of?
choices: A recognized warning sign of predatory behavior
Being polite and never asking personal questions
quiz.explanation: Encouraging secrecy from parents or other trusted adults is one of the clearest, most well-documented warning signs of predatory behavior. A safe adult relationship never depends on hiding the fact that it exists.

quiz.question: Why can a photo posted online reveal where you live, even if you didn't say so?
choices: Photos can secretly contain hidden location data
Photos never contain any extra information
quiz.explanation: Photos often carry hidden 'metadata,' information embedded in the file itself, including the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken. Posting that photo without stripping the metadata can reveal your home address to anyone who knows how to check it.

quiz.question: Why can a passphrase like 'correct-horse-battery-staple' be both stronger and easier to remember than a short complex password?
choices: Its length makes it harder to crack, while being memorable
Long passwords are always weaker than short ones
quiz.explanation: A passphrase's strength comes mainly from its length, so four random unrelated words create far more possible combinations for a hacker to guess than a short password stuffed with symbols. It's also easier for a human brain to remember a string of words than a jumble of characters.

quiz.question: An adult online starts with heavy flattery, then slowly shifts toward secretive topics over weeks. What is this pattern called?
choices: Grooming — a recognized, documented pattern
A completely normal way friendships form
quiz.explanation: Grooming is a gradual, deliberate pattern where an adult builds trust through flattery and attention, then slowly introduces secrecy or inappropriate topics over time. Recognizing the pattern early, and reporting it, matters more than blaming yourself for not seeing it sooner.

quiz.question: A teen feels like it's "too late" to tell anyone about an uncomfortable online relationship that's been going on for months. Is it?
choices: Yes, once time has passed there's no point
No — it's never too late to tell a trusted adult
quiz.explanation: The amount of time that's passed doesn't change how much a trusted adult can still help, whether that means reporting an account, getting support, or just having someone to talk to. Speaking up, even late, deserves support and never judgment.

quiz.question: Besides GPS data in photos, what else can reveal your location?
choices: Check-ins, timestamps, or recognizable details in a video background
Nothing else ever reveals location information
quiz.explanation: Location can leak through more than just photo metadata — a check-in, a timestamp lining up with a known event, or a recognizable street sign in a video background can all pinpoint where you are. Being aware of these less obvious clues matters as much as managing GPS data.

quiz.question: Can a fully private, followers-only account guarantee a post never leaves that circle?
choices: No — a follower could still screenshot and share it
Yes, private accounts are completely leak-proof
quiz.explanation: Privacy settings control who can initially see a post, but they can't control what someone does with it afterward, like taking a screenshot. Once even one trusted follower has seen something, there's no technical way to guarantee it stays contained.

quiz.question: A new online contact makes a small inappropriate request, and when you push back, they apologize but try again differently later. What does this suggest?
choices: They may be testing boundaries, a known grooming tactic
It's a one-time misunderstanding that means nothing
quiz.explanation: Apologizing and then trying a similar request in a different way is a known tactic for testing how much resistance someone will offer before giving in. Recognizing this pattern, rather than dismissing the first request as a one-time mistake, is important for catching manipulation early.

slides.title: Your long-term digital footprint
slides.text: Posts made as a teenager can resurface years later — to college admissions, employers, or anyone who searches your name. For example, a joke posted at 15 that seemed harmless at the time could resurface during a college application review or a job background check years later, in a very different context.

options.label: Old posts always disappear and are never seen again

options.label: What you post as a teenager never has any long-term effect
options.outcome: What you post as a teenager actually can have a real long-term effect, resurfacing in contexts like college admissions.

slides.title: Healthy social media habits
slides.text: Curating your feed, muting accounts that hurt your mood, and taking intentional breaks are all legitimate ways to protect your mental health online. For example, muting or unfollowing accounts that consistently make you feel worse about yourself after scrolling is a genuinely healthy, proactive choice, not something to feel guilty about.

options.outcome: Exactly right! Curating your feed and muting accounts that hurt your mood is a healthy social media habit.

options.label: Keep following it exactly the same since nothing can change
options.outcome: You can actually change what you follow — muting or unfollowing accounts that hurt your mood is a healthy choice.

options.label: Social media never affects how anyone feels
options.outcome: Social media can really affect how people feel — noticing that and adjusting your feed is a healthy response.

slides.title: Digital wellbeing
slides.text: Noticing signs of digital burnout — irritability, trouble sleeping, feeling worse after scrolling — and adjusting your habits is part of genuinely responsible tech use. For example, if you notice you feel consistently more anxious or tired after an hour of scrolling before bed, that's real, useful information worth acting on, not something to ignore.

widgetConfig.scenario: You notice you feel more anxious and tired after an hour of scrolling before bed. What should you do with this?

options.label: Treat it as useful information worth acting on
options.outcome: Exactly right! Noticing signs of digital burnout and adjusting your habits is part of genuinely responsible tech use — that's real, useful information.

options.label: Ignore it since it is not a big deal
options.outcome: Ignoring this feeling skips useful information — noticing and acting on it is part of responsible tech use.

options.label: Feeling worse after scrolling never means anything real
options.outcome: Feeling worse after scrolling can actually mean something real and worth acting on, like adjusting your habits.

slides.title: How apps are designed to keep you scrolling
slides.text: Many apps use techniques like endless scrolling, push notifications, and reward-like features on purpose, to keep you engaged for as long as possible. For example, noticing that turning off non-essential notifications or setting app time limits actually helps you feel more in control, rather than powerless, is a sign the design was working on you before.

widgetConfig.scenario: You open an app "just for a minute" and find yourself scrolling 45 minutes later. What's actually happening?

options.label: Many apps are specifically designed to keep you engaged longer than planned
options.outcome: Exactly — that's not a willpower failure, it's by design. Recognizing the design helps you set intentional limits instead of blaming yourself.

options.label: You just have no self-control
options.outcome: It's not really about willpower — these apps use deliberate design techniques (like infinite scroll and notifications) engineered to maximize time spent.

options.label: This only happens to other people
options.outcome: These design techniques are built to affect everyone — recognizing them is the first step to managing your own screen time intentionally.

slides.title: College admissions and employer searches
slides.text: Many college admissions offices and employers now routinely look up applicants' public social media before making decisions. For example, an admissions officer finding a pattern of publicly posted offensive jokes can factor into a decision, even if the posts were 'just jokes' at the time.

options.label: Delete your accounts entirely right before applying
options.outcome: A more targeted review and cleanup of specific posts is usually more practical than deleting entire accounts.

slides.title: Doing a privacy checkup
slides.text: Periodically reviewing old posts, tagged photos, and privacy settings across your accounts helps you control what your digital footprint actually shows. For example, setting a yearly reminder to review and delete old posts that no longer reflect who you are is a practical habit, not paranoia.

options.outcome: Reviewing old posts periodically isn't excessive — it's a reasonable, practical habit for managing your digital footprint.

options.label: Privacy checkups never reveal anything useful
options.outcome: Privacy checkups actually can reveal useful things, like old posts or photos that no longer reflect who you are.

slides.title: Comparing your life to a highlight reel
slides.text: What people post online is usually a curated highlight reel, not the full picture of their life — comparing your everyday reality to it can distort how you feel. For example, remembering that a friend's seemingly perfect vacation photos leave out the boring or stressful parts of the trip can make scrolling feel less discouraging.

options.label: Comparing your life to curated posts never affects how you feel
options.outcome: Comparing your life to curated posts actually can distort how you feel, which is worth keeping in mind.

slides.title: Turning off what's designed to hook you
slides.text: Features like autoplay, infinite scroll, and streaks are intentionally built to keep you engaged longer than you might choose on your own. For example, turning off autoplay or setting an app timer isn't a sign of weak willpower — it's working around a design built by teams whose job is to maximize your time in-app.

options.label: Yes, needing these tools means you have no self-control
options.outcome: Using these tools isn't a sign of no self-control — it's working around a design intentionally built to keep you engaged longer.

options.label: Autoplay and infinite scroll are never designed to keep you engaged longer
options.outcome: Autoplay and infinite scroll are actually intentionally designed to keep you engaged longer — that's exactly why turning them off helps.

slides.title: Screens and sleep
slides.text: Using screens right before bed, especially bright ones, can make it harder to fall asleep and lower sleep quality, even if you don't notice it immediately. For example, swapping late-night scrolling for a wind-down routine without a screen can measurably improve how rested you feel the next day.

options.label: No, screens before bed never affect sleep at all
options.outcome: Screens before bed actually can affect sleep quite a bit, even if you don't notice it right away.

options.label: Only extremely late screen use before bed has any effect on sleep
options.outcome: Even earlier screen use before bed can affect sleep quality, not just extremely late use.

quiz.question: Why does a long-term digital footprint matter for teenagers?
choices: Old posts can resurface years later to colleges or employers
Nothing posted online ever matters again
quiz.explanation: Posts made as a teenager don't disappear from the internet just because time has passed — they can resurface in a college application review or a job background check years later. A joke that seemed harmless at 15 can look very different in a different context.

quiz.question: What is a sign of possible "digital burnout"?
choices: Feeling worse after scrolling, or trouble sleeping
Feeling exactly the same as always
quiz.explanation: Digital burnout shows up as irritability, trouble sleeping, or feeling worse after scrolling rather than better, even though the activity is supposed to be relaxing. Noticing these physical and emotional signs is the first step toward changing the habit causing them.

quiz.question: Why might an app use endless scrolling and constant notifications?
choices: To keep you engaged and using it longer
To help you use the app less
quiz.explanation: Endless scrolling, push notifications, and small reward-like features are deliberately engineered by design teams to maximize how long users stay engaged with an app. Recognizing that the design is working against your attention makes it easier to push back with tools like time limits.

quiz.question: Why do many college admissions offices and employers look up applicants' social media?
choices: Public posts can factor into their decisions
They are legally forbidden from ever looking
quiz.explanation: Admissions officers and hiring managers routinely search applicants' public social media as part of evaluating character and judgment, not just qualifications. A pattern of offensive posts, even ones intended as jokes, can factor into a real decision about acceptance or employment.

quiz.question: What's the benefit of periodically reviewing old posts and privacy settings?
choices: It helps you control what your digital footprint actually shows
Old posts automatically disappear on their own after enough time
quiz.explanation: A privacy checkup, reviewing old posts, tagged photos, and account settings on a regular schedule, lets you control what your digital footprint actually shows instead of letting years of posts accumulate unchecked. Deleting things that no longer reflect who you are is a practical habit.

quiz.question: Why can comparing your life to what people post online be misleading?
choices: Posts are usually a curated highlight reel, not the full picture
Everything people post online is always the complete, honest truth
quiz.explanation: What people post is typically a curated highlight reel, the best moments chosen and often edited, not a representative sample of their actual day-to-day life. Comparing your ordinary reality to someone else's highlights, like a friend's vacation photos that leave out the stressful parts, can distort how you feel.

quiz.question: Features like autoplay and infinite scroll are designed to...
choices: Keep you engaged and using the app longer
Help you use the app less overall
quiz.explanation: Autoplay and infinite scroll remove natural stopping points, like the end of a video or the bottom of a page, that would otherwise prompt you to pause and decide whether to keep going. Removing those pauses is a deliberate design choice to keep engagement time as high as possible.

quiz.question: Is turning off autoplay or setting an app timer a sign of weak willpower?
choices: Yes, people with strong willpower never need those tools
No — it's working around an intentional design choice
quiz.explanation: Autoplay and similar features are built by teams specifically trying to maximize the time people spend in an app, so resisting them takes more than ordinary willpower. Using a timer or turning off autoplay is working around an engineered system, not a personal failing.

quiz.question: How can screens right before bed affect sleep?
choices: They can make it harder to fall asleep and lower sleep quality
They have no effect on sleep at all
quiz.explanation: Bright screens before bed can suppress melatonin, the hormone that signals your body it's time to sleep, making it harder to fall asleep even if you don't notice it right away. Swapping late-night scrolling for a screen-free wind-down routine can measurably improve how rested you feel.

quiz.question: Muting or unfollowing an account that consistently makes you feel worse after scrolling is...
choices: A legitimate, healthy choice for your mental health
Something to feel guilty about doing
quiz.explanation: Curating a feed by muting or unfollowing accounts that consistently trigger comparison or low mood is an active, healthy way to manage mental health, not something to feel guilty about. Protecting your attention deliberately is a reasonable response to feeds built to capture it.
